newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: U.N envoy says Congo talks to start Thursday.
newsitem.headline: U.N envoy says Congo talks to start Thursday.

text.p: The United Nations envoy to the Congo crisis on Tuesday said talks between representatives of the warring Congolese factions would begin in Gabon's capital, Libreville, on Thursday or Friday.

Mohammed Sahnoun was speaking by phone from Libreville after flying back from a brief visit to the war-torn Congolese capital Brazzaville where a ceasefire he helped to negotiate last week came into effect at midnight on Monday night.

During his brief visit, Sahnoun met with both President Pascal Lissouba and his arch-rival and predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso, and he said despite some shooting on Tuesday the truce between forces loyal to the two rivals appeared to be holding.

"The discussions today were much more positive. There is definitely an eagerness to respect the ceasefire on both sides," he told Reuters. "The delegations are busy preparing for the talks and we hope they will begin in Libreville on Thursday evening or Friday morning," he added.
Some members of the delegations have already arrived in the Gabonese capital, Sahnoun said, and others are due on Wednesday and Thursday.
Street fighting between rival forces loyal to Lissouba and Sassou, both of whom were contenders in scheduled presidential elections due this month, broke out in the Congolese capital six weeks ago.

Since then, numerous ceasefire agreements have been broken, and a previous attempt to bring representatives of both sides to the negotiating table collapsed in Libreville last month before the two sides had even met.
Sahnoun said on Tuesday that any hope of Lissouba and Sassou themselves meeting face to face would depend on the groundwork laId down by their representatives at the talks in Libreville.

He also said he had told both leaders that hopes for the deployment of an international peacekeeping force, requested by both sides, could depend on the spirit in which the talks take place, and the durability of the current ceasefire.
